title: Communicating With Families
answer: A school district once had a problem with truancy notices. The letters sent to families were written in legal language, warning of consequences and citing the education code.

papers.title: Lifting Up Attendance in Rural Districts: A Multi-Site Trial of a Personalized Messaging Campaign
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in 47 rural districts, 16 states: absences down 1.7% to 4.5% at about $4 per student; 0.2 to 0.5 days saved.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence-assisted Translation and Interpretation for Communication With Patients Who Have Language Barriers: A Systematic Review
papers.venue: American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine (abstract)
papers.finding: 18 studies: 62% flagged serious errors; accuracy lower for Haitian Creole and Vietnamese; use professional interpreters when possible.

papers.title: Can Personalized Attendance Information Mitigate Student Absenteeism? Evidence from Six Randomized Field Trials
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: Six district-run RCTs, 78,000 PreK to 12 students: personalized parent messages cut absences 1.9%.

papers.title: Using Existing School Messaging Platforms to Inform Parents about Their Child's Attendance
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in four Atlanta-area districts using existing platforms at zero marginal cost: absences down 2 to 3%; neediest parents hardest to reach.

papers.title: Partnering with immigrant families to promote language justice and equity in education
papers.finding: Focus groups with Spanish, Portuguese, and Cantonese-speaking families: poor interpretation reduced access to special education services and trust in schools.

papers.title: Using Behavioral Insights to Improve School Administrative Communications: The Case of Truancy Notifications
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, N = 131,312: plain-language, supportive truancy notices worked about 40% better than legalistic ones.

papers.title: Reducing Parent-School Information Gaps and Improving Education Outcomes
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in low-income Chilean schools: weekly texts on attendance, grades, and behavior raised math by 0.09 SD.

papers.title: Your Child Missed Learning the Alphabet Today: A Randomized Trial of Sending Teacher-Written Postcards Home to Reduce Absences
papers.venue: Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, 5,552 PreK to grade 2 students: postcards with a teacher note on missed content cut absences 8.3%.

papers.title: Leveraging Parents through Low-Cost Technology
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, middle and high school: weekly automated texts on missed work, grades, and absences cut course failures 27% and raised class attendance 12%.

papers.title: Using behavioral insights to increase attendance at subsidized preschool programs: The Show Up to Grow Up intervention
papers.venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in Chicago subsidized preschools: parent texts cut chronic absence 9.3 percentage points (20%).

papers.title: To Google Translate or not? Newcomer Latino communities in the middle
papers.finding: Vignettes show machine-translated school notices backfiring with Spanish-speaking families; proposes a readability checklist before translating.

papers.title: Reducing Student Absenteeism in the Early Grades by Targeting Parental Beliefs
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT in 10 districts, grades K to 5: parent mailings cut chronic absence 15%.

papers.title: Reducing student absences at scale by targeting parents' misbeliefs
papers.caveat: Single trial; check setting and grade band.
papers.finding: RCT, parents of 28,080 high-risk K-12 students: personalized mailings on total absences cut chronic absence by 10% or more by correcting parents' underestimates.

papers.title: Development of machine translation technology for assisting health communication: A systematic review
papers.caveat: Review quality depends on included studies.
papers.finding: 27 studies: machine translation works best on simple sentences and Western European languages; literature points to MT as a first draft followed by human correction.

children.name: Weekly Updates That Make a Difference
children.blurb: Weekly updates that make a difference are short, specific messages sent to parents about their child's missed assignments, grades, and attendance, often every week.

children.name: Attendance Messages
children.blurb: Attendance messages are simple, personalized communications to families that tell them how many days their child has actually missed, correcting a common underestimate of absences.

children.name: Plain Language
children.blurb: Plain language means rewriting school policies, notices, and forms so families can actually understand them, rather than leaving them in legal or jargon-heavy wording.

children.name: Translation With Human Review
children.blurb: Translation tools let schools reach families in many languages, but they are not perfect and errors can matter.

children.name: Human Interpreters for Sensitive Meetings
children.blurb: Some school conversations are too consequential for machine translation.

children.name: Conferences and Positive Notes
children.blurb: Conferences and positive notes are two family communication practices where AI can help with drafting while the teacher keeps the substance.

children.name: Website Helpers and Resource Directories
children.blurb: A website helper is a chat tool on a district website that answers common family questions about enrollment, schedules, and services at any hour, drawing only on verified district information and admitting when it does not know.

children.name: Emergency Messages
children.blurb: Emergency messages are pre-written, pre-translated templates for situations like lockdowns, weather closures, or bus delays, drafted with AI help and reviewed by people before any crisis occurs.

children.name: Social Media and Media Consent
children.blurb: Schools can use AI to draft social media posts and design graphics, but every student photo shared publicly must first be checked against family consent.

children.name: Engaging Families
children.blurb: Engaging families with AI means using tools to make school communication and family involvement easier, such as grouping survey responses into themes, running parent AI nights, and coordinating volunteers.

children.name: Reaching Families Who Are Hardest to Reach
children.blurb: Schools often fail to reach the families who need them most, because the parents with the greatest needs are the least likely to actually receive school messages.

children.name: Conversation, Not Just Announcements
children.blurb: Two way translated messaging turns school announcements into real conversations, because parents can reply in their own language and get replies in theirs.

children.name: Protecting Family Privacy in Messages
children.blurb: Messages to families often carry protected student information such as grades, absences and behavior, so the tools used to send them must be covered by a signed data privacy agreement.

children.name: Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask
children.blurb: Every parent should be able to ask five questions about how their child's school uses AI: which tools touch a child's information, whether signed agreements cover those tools, who makes decisions about a child, how the school teaches children to use AI well, and what a parent can do with a concern.

sections.body: This part of school life is how a school or district talks with the families it serves, through notices, updates, attendance letters, translations, conferences, websites, emergency alerts, social media and everyday engagement. The book describes AI doing practical work here: drafting messages in plain language, translating them into families' languages, and summarizing long documents so families can act on them. It also names the risks, including translations that mislead, chat tools that fail, and messages sent without the care they deserve. The chapter's frame is that how schools communicate affects what families do, and that small changes in wording can have large effects. The research on family communication is among the strongest in this Volume, with several randomized trials showing that clear, frequent, personal messages improve attendance and grades.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works, as the book reports it, is plain, supportive, personal communication, including rewritten truancy notices that outperformed legalistic ones, personalized attendance messages, teacher-written postcards about missed content, and weekly texts about attendance, grades and behavior. What does not work is unchecked translation, where a notice goes out through a tool without review and says something different from the original, and poor interpretation, which damages trust and reduces access to services, falling hardest on the families the district most needs to reach. The book also notes that message counts alone do not show quality, and that the neediest parents are the hardest to reach. The rule it holds to is simple: AI drafts, and a person owns every word that matters, with human review and interpreters required for anything critical.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages move from routine to sensitive to structural. Weekly Updates That Make a Difference and Attendance Messages cover the regular, evidence-backed messages that improve attendance and grades, while Plain Language explains the wording that makes them land. Translation With Human Review and Human Interpreters for Sensitive Meetings carry the chapter's central caution and its rule, and Conferences and Positive Notes, Website Helpers and Resource Directories, Emergency Messages, and Social Media and Media Consent extend communication into meetings, public information and urgent situations. Engaging Families, Reaching Families Who Are Hardest to Reach, and Conversation, Not Just Announcements push past one-way announcements toward real relationship, and Protecting Family Privacy in Messages guards the trust that work depends on. Five Questions Every Parent Should Ask closes the set as the tool families can use to hold a school accountable. A teacher would go to the update, attendance and positive note pages for daily practice, a leader to translation, interpreters, emergency messages and privacy for district rules and review, and a parent to the five questions and the engagement pages to know what to ask and expect.
